full_judgment:
2. Opposite parties as plaintiffs instituted SCC Suit No.9 of 2005 in the said Court of SCC Judge for ejectment of the petitioner. The suit was decreed ex parte by judgment and decree dated 8-11-05. Then, the petitioner made an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure hereinafter referred to as the Code being Miscellaneous Appeal No.18 of 2006 for restoration of the suit to its original file and number after setting aside the ex parte decree. 

 3. Opposite parties first opposed the application by filing a written objection. The miscellaneous case was however, allowed on compromise by the Court by an order dated 8-2-07 subject to payment of cost of Taka 1,200 to the plaintiffs by 5-3-07. As the petitioner did not make the deposit within the time, the trial Court by its order dated 11-3-07 set aside said order dated 8-2-07 upon an application made on behalf of the opposite parties. 

 11. An affidavit-in-opposition was filed on behalf of the opposite parties opposing the Rule. In the said affidavit, it is stated that the order restoring the suit to its original file and number was passed by the Court on the basis of a compromise between the parties and, as such, the Court was not competent to extend the agreed time. 

 13. The petitioner is a defaulter and has taken dilatory tactics in delaying disposal of the suit. He allowed the suit to be decreed ex parte. When the petitioner made application for setting aside the ex parte decree, the opposite parties readily agreed to hearing of the suit in presence of the petitioner and a conditional order was passed on compromise. Since the order was passed on compromise between the parties, the Court cannot compel the opposite parties to accept the cost beyond the period as they agreed. The conduct of the petitioner is not fair and he is trying to continue staying in the suit premises most illegally and, as such, is not entitled to any relief in the Rule. 

 16. Mr Mahbubey Alam, learned Senior Advocate for the opposite parties, submitted that order dated 8-2-07, which set aside the ex parte decree and restored the suit to its original file and number was a conditional order as agreed by the parties that is subject to deposit by the petitioner cost of Taka 1,200 by 5-3-07 and in default, the order stood disallowed. 

 21. The facts as stated hereinabove do not need to be reiterated. What is not disputed is that on 8-11-05 the aforesaid suit was decreed ex parte. Whereupon, the petitioner made an application under Order IX, rule 13 of the Code for restoration of the suit to its original file and number after setting aside the ex parte decree. 

 29. In the case before the Appellate Division, the Government of Bangladesh made an inadvertent error by referring to a wrong section of the Army Act in taking the impugned action, which was subsequently regularised by passing subsequent order making it effective from the same date of earlier order. In the facts of the case before me, I find no application for the aforesaid authority at all. The impugned order is challenged. before me by reference to section 148 of the Code only though in the application dated 19-3-07 no case was made out under the section nor was extension of the time sought for thereunder. There is also no dispute that order dated 8-2-07 was passed on the basis of a compromise arrived at by the parties and the ex parte decree was set aside and the suit restored to its file and number subject to the condition of payment of cost of Taka 1,200 by the petitioner to the opposite parties by the agreed date 5-3-07. 

 "Only after complying with the order said above ex parte decree dated 8-11-06 be hereby set aside and the same be restored to its original file and number. In csee of failure, the instant order shall stand disallowed." 

 33. Scope of section 148 of the Code is now well settled by the authorities of superior Courts of the Subcontinent. Perusal of section 148 makes it clear that where any period is fixed or granted by the Court for doing of an act, the Court may, in its discretion, enlarge such period of time even after the expiry of the period originally fixed or granted. Only exception to such general principle is when the period is fixed or granted by the Court on the basis of the period prescribed by any law, the Court then would have no power to extend such period of time under the section. Similarly, when the Court fixes a period of time for doing an act on the basis of an agreement or a compromise arrived at by the parties, it would have generally no jurisdiction to override the agreement of the parties. 

 "In the case before us, the situation is totally different. Unlike the case of Hukum- chand vs Bansilal where there was a statutory compulsion to confirm the sale on the dismissal of the application under Order XXI, rule 90 and, therefore, postponement and further. postponement of the confirmation of the sale could only be by the consent of the parties, in the case before us, there was no statutory compulsion to dismiss the application under Order XXI, rule 90 in the absence of an agreement between the parties. The Court would have then decided the appeal arising out of the application on merits. The parties, however, entered into a compromise and invited the Court to make an order in terms of the compromise, which the Court did. The time for deposit stipulated by the parties became the time allowed by the Court and this gave the Court the jurisdiction to extend time in appropriate cases. Of course, time would not be extended ordinarily, nor for the mere asking. It would be granted in rare cases to prevent manifest injustice. True the Court would not rewrite a contract between the parties but the Court would relieve against a forfeiture clause, And, where the contract between the parties had merged in the order of the Court, the Court's freedom to act to further the ends of justice would surely not stand curtailed. Nothing said in Hukumchand case militates against this view."
